This paper introduces a novel, data-centric methodology that evaluates the hardware suitability for key problems within sequential and benchmark datasets during various stages of the training process for Simple Neural Unit (SNU) networks. Specifically, we focus on exploring the performance characteristics required for processing spatio-temporal sequences with high efficiency using an approach that balances spatial and temporal dimensions across different dataset requirements. support critical decisions concerning human safety, with machine learning (ML) serving as a prominent subset for decision support. However, potential biases in training data or models pose significant risks, potentially resulting in inappropriate outcomes. While various diagnostic methods exist to identify such biases by estimating or measuring them post-training, post-deployment regulation necessitates pre-trained model validation tools. Although some recent efforts have introduced a unified framework to locate, quantify, and mitigate bias using paired protected and group-of-interest attributes, these methods often rely on extensive computation. Furthermore, these heuristic-based approaches lack transparency, offering no guarantees that protected groups will receive favorable decisions. In this paper, we introduce a novel method for transferring bias correction from standard classification tasks at inference time. Our approach employs an optimized classification decision network trained on both safe and non-safe attributes to adjust output class probabilities in real-time during inference based on input attributes. Experimental results across multiple datasets demonstrate that our method achieves similar performance compared to heavier heuristic methods while significantly reducing bias during inference with higher efficiency on protected attributes.

Search has proven effective in solving complex games. To achieve optimal deep learning outcomes, the quality of labeled training data is paramount; thus, improving labeled data is essential. This study introduces labeled domain-adaptive adaptive adversarial adaptation (D4S), which enhances labeled data through a linear adapter trained via adversarial adaptation. In D4S, an adapter modifies inputs provided by a source domain—such as AI-generated playthroughs—to generate synthetic data closer to human behavior (the target domain). The source and target domains both employ identical neural networks configured for differential privacy, ensuring D4S produces high-fidelity human-like data while restricting access to actual human interaction records due to privacy constraints. Empirical assessments using Go games indicate that D4S effectively mitigates performance gaps in artificial data, yielding significant improvements over raw source data.
